title: A Secret Strategy That Makes Classroom Management Easier anagement-easier/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin explains how identifying and quietly enlisting natural student leaders can make classroom management easier. During the first weeks of school he seeks out the two or three students other kids look up to, regardless of whether they are top academic performers, and asks them privately to help by modeling friendliness and being first to follow directions. He illustrates the approach with a story about protecting a vulnerable student named Laura from bullying by asking a respected classmate to quietly act as her protective friend. Linsin argues that when these informal leaders are the first to comply and encourage classmates to do the same, the rest of the class follows more quickly. He cautions that the strategy only works if the teacher is also a genuine leader whom students trust, respect, and admire, since otherwise the recruited students will be ineffective or even use their influence negatively.
points: Identify two or three natural student leaders early in the year based on peer influence, not necessarily academic performance or past behavior.
Recruit these students privately and informally to model positive behaviors like encouragement, friendship, and being first to follow directions.
Use a trusted student leader to quietly protect a vulnerable classmate, as Linsin did to stop bullying against a student named Laura.
Leverage leaders to gradually bring reluctant or difficult students on board until they become outnumbered and give in.
Recognize that this strategy only works if the teacher has first earned genuine trust, respect, and admiration from students.
quotes: During the first few weeks of a new school year, I try to identify students with natural leadership ability. Typically, two or three strong leaders will emerge from a class of thirty.
This doesn’t mean that these natural leaders are top students or that they’ve been particularly well behaved in the past (sometimes it’s better if they’re not).
I didn’t ask this student to hang out with Laura, nor did she. I just asked her to keep an eye on her and act like a protective big sister.
As a result, Laura was never picked on, made fun of, or meant to feel less than a valued member of the classroom. Predictably, she blossomed.
I’ve discovered that identifying student leaders early and soliciting their help as role models gets the rest of the class on board quicker—and helps keep them there.
Identifying leaders willing to influence other students can make classroom management easier. But there is a catch. You must also be a leader.
Students with leadership ability are going to use it. And if you don’t help them direct it in a positive way, it may not always be used for good.
